<reason>Side A (CON) won the decisive exchanges. A's arithmetic pressure—mid-budget originals carrying near-blockbuster break-even via marketing exposure while retaining a lower ceiling—was conceded by B but never answered with pricing. B's refusal to supply any hit-rate threshold was framed as epistemic honesty, but A correctly leveraged it: "benefits asserted, costs conceded, arithmetic declined." A's burden allocation ("I don't have to prove sequels more profitable, only that PRO hasn't shown originals are") is legitimate given the proposition puts the spending-shift burden on PRO. B's best counter—that A equally failed to price the sequel side—landed but was blunted by A's burden response and the cushioning factors (audience floor, merchandising, pre-sales). The acquisition dilemma and the "status quo dressed as reform" charge were sharp; B's reply that selection and allocation are different decisions was adequate but not decisive. B maintained the motion as written and kept a coherent harvest/planting frame, with clean A1/A2 structure and disciplined refusal to fake numbers—real strengths. But A created more live pressure and resolved the choice more clearly. Execution costs for A: two clipped turns.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Pressure Question 1 demanding a hit-rate number, followed by B's explicit refusal to supply one and A's Rebuttal 2 levering that refusal—"benefits listed without prices... uncertainty that isn't priced isn't an investment thesis"—was the most decisive exchange, crystallizing the entire burden clash.</best_rebuttal>
